meta.title: Download ai-memory and read the changelog
meta.description: Download ai-memory {tag} for Linux, macOS and Windows, or install it with mise, the AUR or Docker. Checksums, release history and the full changelog.

hero.title: Download ai-memory {tag}
hero.lede: Released {date}. One self-contained binary per platform, each with a SHA-256 checksum next to it. MIT licensed.

builds.title: Binaries
builds.after: After unpacking, follow the setup guide: install the binary, configure the server, then launch your agent.

mac.note: Includes a launchd agent. If you download with a browser, clear the quarantine flag first.

win.note: Experimental. WSL2 with the Linux build is the supported path. Scoop installs this same zip.

builds.upgrade: Later, a binary under a writable prefix (Linux, macOS, the Windows zip) updates itself with ai-memory upgrade: it downloads the matching release, verifies the checksum and refreshes the hooks. Packages update through their package manager.
builds.upgradeNote: Coming from 2.x? Back up the wiki and database before upgrading the server, then update clients. Migrations are forward-only; rollback needs the old binary and backup. Read the 3.0 upgrade steps.

channels.title: Package managers and containers

mise.title: mise
mise.note: Linux and macOS. Verifies the checksum for you. New releases can take about a day to appear.

aur.title: Arch Linux (AUR)
aur.note: Installs systemd units for a user or a system service.

brew.title: Homebrew
brew.note: macOS and Linux, including atomic distributions where Homebrew is the usual way to add command-line tools. Then use ai-memory setup or brew services start ai-memory, not both.

rpm.title: Fedora (RPM)
rpm.note: x86_64 and aarch64 packages with the binary, the hook sources and the systemd units. Then follow the user or system service steps.

scoop.title: Windows (Scoop)
scoop.note: Adds the maintainer's bucket, checks the zip against the checksum published with the release and puts ai-memory on PATH. Update with scoop update ai-memory; the built-in self-upgrade refuses a Scoop install.

docker.title: Docker or Podman
docker.note: Multi-arch: linux/amd64 and linux/arm64, so Apple Silicon needs no emulation.

src.title: From source
src.note: Needs the Rust toolchain pinned in rust-toolchain.toml.

channels.clients: Client machines that only send hooks to a remote server do not need the full binary. The release also ships ai-memory-install-hooks and wrapper scripts for Docker on Linux, macOS and Windows. They are listed on the release page.

changelog.title: What changed
changelog.lede: A short summary of the newest release, then the counts for the ones before it. The full changelog on GitHub has every entry.
changelog.stale: The summary for {tag} is being written. The counts below cover it, and the full changelog has every entry.

highlights.title: The interface now looks like this site
highlights.text: The built-in web UI and the management console moved to this site's palette and typefaces: mineral paper and graphite in both themes, squared 2px controls, amber buttons, line icons in place of Unicode symbols, and the smallest text a couple of points larger. Routes and markup are unchanged. The binary also carries 24 Brazilian Portuguese guides and serves them when the interface language is pt-BR.

highlights.title: Install with Homebrew
highlights.text: brew install akitaonrails/tap/ai-memory installs the release binary and its hook sources on macOS and on Linux, which is how atomic distributions such as Bazzite and Fedora Silverblue usually add command-line tools. Use ai-memory setup or brew services start ai-memory, not both.

highlights.title: Tencent WorkBuddy is supported
highlights.text: Hooks for six events, an HTTP MCP entry and managed skills, and setup finds WorkBuddy on its own. Approve the ai-memory server in WorkBuddy's custom connector settings after installing, and close a finished session with ai-memory finalize-session --agent workbuddy, because WorkBuddy fires no session end.

highlights.title: Gemini billed to your Google Cloud project
highlights.text: The new vertex provider calls the same Gemini models through Vertex AI, where Google Cloud credit pays for them. It signs in with Application Default Credentials, from gcloud or a service-account key, and two environment variables choose the project and the region.

highlights.title: Ask for only the confident results
highlights.text: memory_query takes a min_relevance floor that drops weak hits before the count limit, and a project can set that floor and its own default number of results in its .ai-memory.toml. The floor needs a reranker; when nothing is scored, the hits come back unfiltered with a note rather than empty.

highlights.title: Look at what retrieval returned
highlights.text: Turn on retrieval history and every query records its scope, its filters, how long it took and each page it returned with that page's score and ranking explanation, on a read-only page linked from the session timeline. Compiled pages now also record the observations they were built from.

highlights.title: Smaller switches
highlights.text: Reach every MCP tool from a shell with ai-memory call, fix the language of generated prose, keep a launcher's generated prompts out of the cross-project profile, re-brief when a session moves into another project, run the LLM contradiction pass on its own cadence, page through a full inbox, and let ai-memory doctor warn when another local account can write the data directory.
